newsitem.title: LEBANON: Market bullish on Solidere changes.
newsitem.headline: Market bullish on Solidere changes.

text.p: Solidere shares were at a seven-month high on Thursday after Lebanon's biggest company said it would lift ownership restrictions and allow foreign investors and local institutions to buy them.
Solidere A shares rose to $12 to match the B shares. Representatives of local and foreign finance houses forecast strong foreign and local interest when the ownership changes took place in October.
"We would expect a lot of demand for the A and B shares and we have a long-term target share price of $25," Dominic Herbert, Beirut representative of Robert Fleming Holdigs Ltd, said.

"This is very positive for the stock," Anthony Tarazi, head of treasury and capital markets at Beirut finance house Lebanon Invest, told Reuters. "We would think that it should give a strong boost to the price at least when it happens in October, and it should start now.
"The shares will attract tremendous interest both from abroad and from Lebanese institutions," he added.

Solidere chairman Nasser Chammaa said in an interview with Reuters the changes would be made in October when the lengthy process of distributing 100 million A shares to property owners in central Beirut was expected to be complete.
The flood of A shares released on the market since 1994 has helped to depress Solidere's shares and Chamma said he would not introduce the ownership changes until distribution was complete.

With a market capitalisation of nearly $2 billion, Solidere is by far the biggest company on the fledgling Beirut Stock Exchange. Chammaa said the changes would benefit the market -- which lists 10 shares -- because foreigners who invested in Solidere would look for other Lebanese shares.
"Institutional investors like to set up a portfolio in a country, not just in one company," he said. "This will definitely be a big plus for the capital markets in Lebanon."
Solidere shares have languished around all-time lows in recent months despite a widely held market view that Solidere's fundamentals are good and the shares are heavily undervalued.
Chammaa said the board would announce next week the date of a shareholders' meeting to approve proposals for lifting the ownership restrictions, which would also need government approval.

Shares in Solidere, flagship of Lebanon's postwar reconstruction, cannot at present be owned by non-Arabs. Lebanese banks and financial institutions and local companies with foreign shareholders are also barred from ownership.
When the ownership changes are made, "there will be no restrictions on transferability except for the 10 percent limit on ownership of the company's shares by a single owner," Chammaa said.

Solidere began rebuilding the war-ravaged centre of Beirut in 1994. Infrastructure work is due for completion in August 1998 and Solidere is already putting up new buildings and selling plots for development.
The 1.8 million square metres project on the Mediterranean seafront is described as the major urban redevelopment of the 1990s.

Chammaa said the success of Solidere's GDRs, which are trading on the London Stock Exchange at $16-17, well above the price of the underlying shares on the Beirut bourse, indicated the appetite for the company's shares among foreign institutions.

Chammaa said he did not expect the changes to have a negative affect on the GDRs. However, Herbert of Flemings said they could fall in the coming week but he expected them to maintain a small premium over the underlying shares.
